Published online:
2026-09-02

Geographic focus:
Middle East (Qatar, UAE, Oman, Strait of Hormuz), Asia (India, Japan), Singapore (dateline)

Temporal focus:
T1. Historical report [YES] — Documents STS transfers that occurred in July–August 2026
T2. Forward-looking reporting short-term risks (next few weeks/months) [YES] — Ongoing Hormuz disruption, continued LNG supply constraints, elevated spot prices
T3. Forward-looking reporting long-term risks (next quarters/years) [NO]

Synopsis:
Since a US-Israeli war on Iran erupted on February 28, Iran has largely shut the Strait of Hormuz, severely disrupting LNG flows from Qatar and the UAE. In response, at least three LNG cargoes have been routed via ship-to-ship (STS) transfers outside the strait — an unusual workaround for LNG logistics. Key incidents involve vessels GasLog Shanghai (damaged exiting Hormuz), Al Rekayyat (hit by a projectile), and Mraweh (ADNOC-controlled). Cargoes are ultimately reaching India and Japan but with significant delays and added operational complexity. Asian spot LNG prices have surged to $23.20/mmBtu, more than double pre-conflict levels, reflecting reduced regional LNG export volumes.

---

**Q01. Relevance to EU energy / German power market?**
Relevance: IMPLICIT
While the article focuses on Asia-Pacific LNG flows, the Hormuz closure structurally tightens the global LNG supply pool. Europe — and Germany specifically — competes with Asian buyers for LNG on the spot market. Sustained Middle East LNG disruption reduces the global supply available to European terminals, exerting upward pressure on TTF gas prices, which in turn drives German power prices higher via gas-fired generation marginal cost setting.

---

**Q02. New vs. known information?**
Risk score: 45 / 100
The Iran-Hormuz disruption has been ongoing since late February and is not new. However, the specific detail of LNG STS transfers — an operationally unusual and costly workaround — signals that the disruption is more entrenched and structurally damaging than a short-term closure. The $23.20/mmBtu Asian spot price (2×+ pre-conflict levels) and damage to specific named vessels add meaningful new granularity to an already known risk.

---

**Q03. Explicit bullish impact on German power futures?**
Explicit: NO
Impact score: 30 / 100
No direct reference to European or German power markets. The bullish transmission is implicit: tighter global LNG supply → higher TTF → higher German power prices. The impact is real but indirect and already partially priced in given the conflict has been ongoing for six months.

---

**Q04. Explicit bearish impact on German power futures?**
Explicit: NO
Impact score: 5 / 100
No bearish signal for German power. STS workarounds marginally ease supply tightness for Asian buyers but do not meaningfully increase supply available to Europe. No bearish case is present in this article.
